solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: End-of-season nerves make my sub quite erratic

indicators.note: erratic means wandering and irregular, so the letters of the five words before it are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A football manager frets that a substitute is playing unpredictably as the season nears its tense end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erratic' rearranges MAKE MY SUB QUITE. The phrase was coined by Alex Ferguson, a British football manager, for the tense final weeks of a league season.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial British football idiom for the anxious closing stage of a title or relegation race.

clue.text: Guess our health will suffer here!

definitions.text: Guess our health will suffer here!

indicators.note: to suffer is to be damaged or knocked about, so the letters of the three words before it are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A grim warning that some place will be bad for our wellbeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will suffer' rearranges GUESS OUR HEALTH; the whole clue also describes the place, where an animal's health suffers terminally.
explanation.definitionFit: An abattoir is where livestock are killed, so health suffers there in the most final way.

clue.text: In ruins, as we agreed, regularly in the dark

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the words before it is taken

explanation.surface: Someone in a wrecked state agrees without understanding what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link word; 'regularly' takes the even letters of 'ruins as we agreed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be kept in the dark is an idiom for being ignorant of something, uninformed.

clue.text: A silly sailor making sketch

parts.note: dumb is an informal word for silly or stupid
a rating is a naval sailor without a commission

explanation.surface: A foolish seaman is drawing a rough picture.
explanation.walkthrough: RATING, a non-commissioned sailor, is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: To adumbrate is to outline or give a faint sketch, so drawing a sketch fits the participle.

clue.text: Nice girl gets year with short F1 driver

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the surname loses its final letter

parts.note: Sebastian Vettel was a Formula One world champion driver

explanation.surface: A girl joins up with a Formula One racer for a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is the French city, not the adjective: a girl's name from France. 'short' docks the last L of VETTEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A French female first name, the kind of girl you might meet in the Riviera city.

clue.text: M Clunes, a comic in America

indicators.note: comic means funny or absurd, so these letters are rearranged in a ludicrous way

explanation.surface: Martin Clunes, the British actor, plays a comedian in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic' rearranges M CLUNES A; 'in' is a link word. Martin Clunes is a British TV actor.
explanation.definitionFit: The bearded figure in a top hat is the traditional personification of the United States.

clue.text: It can be climbed in short order

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the words short order, spanning the gap

explanation.surface: Something can be scaled very quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short order' looks like an idiom for 'quickly'; 'in' is the hiding signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocky hill or peak, especially on Dartmoor, is something walkers climb.

clue.text: Negligible car sickness?

parts.note: the Mini is a classic small British car
mal is French for illness, as in mal de mer

explanation.surface: A question about whether motion sickness in a car is trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: MINI is a small British car; MAL is a French word for sickness, familiar from 'mal de mer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something so small in amount that it hardly counts.

clue.text: French epic poetry, song and dance, these works

indicators.note: works here is a verb meaning knocks into shape, so the letters of the fodder words are reshaped

explanation.surface: A list of artistic works: French epic verse, music, dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' looks like a noun for art but rearranges SONG, DANCE and THESE; 'and' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The medieval French verse epics celebrating heroic deeds, like the Chanson de Roland.

clue.text: An offer to host game, usually

indicators.note: to host is to have a guest inside, so one piece holds the other within it

parts.note: a sale is an offering of goods to buyers
RU is short for rugby union

explanation.surface: Normally, an offer is made to stage some sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' is rugby union, abbreviated; 'offer' is a noun here, an offering of goods for sale.
explanation.definitionFit: Generally, in the normal course of things, a set phrase meaning normally.

clue.text: Fancy one being given unlimited port

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like fancy that!
I is the Roman numeral for one
nth means to any degree, without limit, as in to the nth degree

explanation.surface: Someone imagines having endless access to a fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' is an exclamation of surprise, COR in British slang; 'being given' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek city on the isthmus, historically a major trading harbour.

clue.text: Travel agent's first choice in India?

parts.note: to go is to travel

indicators.note: first picks out only the opening letter of the word agent's

explanation.surface: Where would a travel agent first recommend visiting in India?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as an example: one destination you might choose in India.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal Indian state famous with holidaymakers for its beaches, a popular travel pick.

clue.text: Bird crosses empty lake, needing second drink

indicators.note: crosses means goes across, so the bird spans the other letters, taking them inside it

parts.note: the bittern is a wading bird of the heron family

indicators.note: empty means hollowed out, so only the outside letters of lake remain

parts.note: mo is a short moment, a second

explanation.surface: A wading bird flies over a dried-up lake and needs a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crosses' looks like flying over, but means the bird's letters straddle the others; 'needing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbonated soft drink flavoured with lemon and quinine, often a mixer.

clue.text: One invention designed to show up others?

definitions.text: One invention designed to show up others?

parts.words: One invention designed to show up others?
parts.note: invention here means a made-up story, so the device is built to expose other fabrications

explanation.surface: A gadget made to outshine other inventions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invention' reads as a gadget, but also means a lie: the device exposes other lies, and is itself an invention.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygraph is a machine claimed to reveal when a subject tells untruths.

clue.text: Bone-cutting saw in theatre with leather covering

indicators.note: covering means wrapped around, so one piece goes outside the other

parts.note: to tan is to turn hide into leather
rep is short for repertory theatre

explanation.surface: A surgical saw kept in a theatre, wrapped in leather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' suggests an operating theatre, apt for a skull saw, but means repertory theatre; 'leather' is a verb, to tan.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical instrument with a circular blade used to cut holes in the skull.

clue.text: Station's wet facilities

parts.note: to water something is to wet it
facilities is a euphemism for a toilet, the loo

explanation.surface: A railway station has damp toilets.
explanation.walkthrough: LOO is British slang for toilet; Waterloo is a major London railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: A large London railway terminus, named after the 1815 battle.

clue.text: Trick panellist, as magician

parts.note: a con is a swindle or trick
a juror sits on a panel, the jury

explanation.surface: A quiz-show panellist tricks people while posing as a conjuror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer of illusions and sleight of hand, a stage magic act.

clue.text: Doctor of law not about to waffle

parts.note: a rabbi is a teacher of Jewish law

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word not is read backwards

explanation.surface: A legal scholar refuses to talk nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor of law' is a rabbi, a teacher of Jewish law; 'about' turns NOT to TON.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom for talking at length about nothing much, chattering on.

clue.text: Run after black bag

indicators.note: after places the run piece behind the black piece

parts.note: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black
a ladder is a run in a stocking or tights

explanation.surface: Someone sprints after a black handbag.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder is British usage for a run in tights.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable sac, as in a football's inner bladder or the body's bag for urine.

clue.text: Familiar 21 for hostile daughter

indicators.note: the answer to 21 down, read as tip off, says to take off the leading letter

parts.note: averse means opposed or hostile

explanation.surface: A cross-reference clue: a familiar warning about a hostile daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 21's answer literally as 'remove the tip': AVERSE loses its first letter, then D follows; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be versed in something is to be knowledgeable about it, acquainted with it.

clue.text: Rest of 22 in 12, ultimately

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation within the synonym of the first word

parts.note: the first word of 12 across means sour, and its second word ends the wordplay
OJ is the usual abbreviation for the drink at 22 across

indicators.note: ultimately picks only the last letter of the second word of 12 across

parts.note: the first word of 12 across means sour, and its second word ends the wordplay

explanation.surface: A cross-reference recipe of one drink inside another.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is BITTER LEMON: BITTER gives SOUR, which holds OJ (22 is ORANGE JUICE), and 'ultimately' takes N from LEMON.
explanation.definitionFit: A sojourn is a temporary stay somewhere, a break or pause from travelling.

clue.text: Row over humourless clue?

indicators.note: over means lying across, so the quarrel sits around the other piece

parts.note: a tiff is a petty quarrel
po, as in po-faced, means solemn and humourless

explanation.surface: An argument erupts over a joyless crossword hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'humourless' points to the British word 'po-faced', solemn; 'over' means the quarrel goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip-off is a private hint or warning, so a clue in the sense of information.

clue.text: Over near 23, fluid to freeze drink

parts.note: O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for over

indicators.note: fluid means flowing and changeable, so the letters of near with the prison word are rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 23 across is a word for prison, used here as letters
to ice something is to freeze it

explanation.surface: A cross-reference recipe for chilling a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fluid' rearranges NEAR plus JUG (23 across) into RANGEJU.
explanation.definitionFit: The squeezed citrus drink is a common breakfast beverage.

clue.text: Prison psychologist taking November off

indicators.note: off, with taking, means removed, so a letter is dropped from the surname

parts.note: Carl Jung was the Swiss founder of analytical psychology
N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A prison psychologist takes a month's leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking ... off' removes N (November in the phonetic alphabet) from JUNG; 'jug' is British slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for jail, from the old sense of a stone strongroom.

clue.text: Mixed cider as cocktail

indicators.note: mixed means stirred together, so the letters of cider and as are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: A drink of blended cider served as a mixed drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' rearranges CIDER AS.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic mixed drink of brandy, orange liqueur and lemon juice.

clue.text: An officer's function

parts.note: CO is short for commanding officer
the possessive ending supplies its letter

explanation.surface: A question of what a military officer's role is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'function' reads as duty but means the trigonometric function, the cosine.
explanation.definitionFit: Cos is the standard abbreviation for cosine, a trigonometric ratio.

clue.text: Beats unconscious — the reverse of 'warm'

parts.note: out means knocked out, unconscious

indicators.note: the reverse of tells us to read the synonym backwards

parts.note: snug means cosily warm

explanation.surface: Someone beats an unconscious opponent, the opposite of keeping warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the reverse of' looks like it wants an antonym, but turns SNUG back to GUNS.
explanation.definitionFit: To have more firepower than someone, figuratively to beat or outdo them.

clue.text: Look here, it says 'X marks the spot'?

parts.note: the letter X is shaped like a cross
a map reference pinpoints a location

explanation.surface: A treasure-map caption: here is where X marks the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it says' is a link; the definition is the instruction a cross-reference gives a reader.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-reference is a note directing the reader to look at another place in the text.
